What It Is: Vehicle Inspection is the controls for safe, lawful and traceable storage, fleet, transport, drivers, cargo and dangerous goods. Within Fleet Compliance, it defines the obligation, accountable roles, control activities and evidence needed to demonstrate conformity.
Why It Is Important: It protects people, cargo, product integrity and delivery continuity and prevents road, warehouse, customs, security and insurance incidents.
Why It Is Needed: It is needed by road/transport law, licences and fitness requirements, dangerous-goods rules, warehouse/product controls and customer/insurance conditions. Primary catalogue basis: ISO 39001. Applicability must be validated for the specific SBU, entity, site, product, activity and jurisdiction.
How It Should Work: Maintain approved vehicles/drivers/carriers and documents; perform pre-use and fitness checks; control loading/routes/hours/speed; secure and trace cargo; manage dangerous goods and warehouse conditions; monitor incidents and maintenance. Link the source → obligation → risk → control → owner → due date → evidence → testing → finding/CAPA → management review.
Minimum Requirements for Compliance: Keep vehicle/driver/carrier register; verify licence, fitness, insurance and competence; inspect before dispatch; plan safe route/load; control hours/speed/GPS; secure and document custody; segregate dangerous goods; maintain temperature/warehouse where required; inspect/maintain; report/investigate incidents; block expired/unsafe dispatch. Universal CMS controls: assign a unique ID; document applicability and source; obtain Legal approval for legal interpretations; name owner/reviewer/approver; define frequency and due date; prevent closure without evidence; retain audit trail; escalate exceptions; complete CAPA and independent effectiveness retest.
Required Evidence: Registration, fitness, insurance, driver licence/competence, carrier approval, pre-use and maintenance records, GPS/route/hour logs, load and custody documents, dangerous-goods papers, warehouse/temperature logs, incidents and CAPA. Evidence must be authentic, current, attributable, approved where required, protected and retrievable.
Audit / Pass Criteria: Pass only when vehicle/driver/carrier and cargo documents are valid, safety and custody controls operate for every sampled movement, conditions are maintained and incidents are effectively managed. A COMPLIANT conclusion requires both effective design and effective operation, current sufficient evidence for the full in-scope period, and no unresolved mandatory or critical/high breach. Missing material evidence means NOT DEMONSTRATED, not compliant.
Non-Compliance Triggers: Failure includes expired fitness/licence/insurance, unsafe vehicle/driver, overload or hours breach, unsecured/untraceable cargo, temperature excursion, dangerous-goods error, unauthorized carrier or uninvestigated incident.
Typical Applicability / SBU: Company and contractor vehicles and drivers

What It Is: GRI is the governance, due diligence, measurement and disclosure of material environmental, social and governance impacts, risks and commitments. Within Sustainability Reporting, it defines the obligation, accountable roles, control activities and evidence needed to demonstrate conformity.
Why It Is Important: It supports stakeholder trust, financing and buyer access and prevents misleading claims, unmanaged human-rights/climate risk and unreliable disclosures.
Why It Is Needed: It is needed by adopted GRI/ISSB/SASB standards, contracts, lender/buyer requirements, board commitments and applicable sustainability law. Primary catalogue basis: GRI; ISSB; IFRS S1; IFRS S2; CSRD. Applicability must be validated for the specific SBU, entity, site, product, activity and jurisdiction.
How It Should Work: Conduct materiality and due diligence; define boundaries/methods; assign data owners; implement controls; monitor KPIs; address adverse impacts; reconcile and assure disclosures; approve claims; review progress and CAPA. Link the source → obligation → risk → control → owner → due date → evidence → testing → finding/CAPA → management review.
Minimum Requirements for Compliance: Identify applicable standards and stakeholders; assess material topics and impacts; set governance/policies/targets; map metrics and methodology; control source data and estimates; conduct human-rights/environmental due diligence; remediate impacts; review/approve disclosure; obtain assurance where required; prevent greenwashing. Universal CMS controls: assign a unique ID; document applicability and source; obtain Legal approval for legal interpretations; name owner/reviewer/approver; define frequency and due date; prevent closure without evidence; retain audit trail; escalate exceptions; complete CAPA and independent effectiveness retest.
Required Evidence: Materiality and due-diligence records, policies/targets, metric dictionary, source data and calculations, GHG/water/social evidence, stakeholder engagement, remediation, review/approval, assurance and published report. Evidence must be authentic, current, attributable, approved where required, protected and retrievable.
Audit / Pass Criteria: Pass only when scope and methods match the chosen framework, data is complete and traceable, material impacts are governed, claims are substantiated and disclosures pass review/assurance. A COMPLIANT conclusion requires both effective design and effective operation, current sufficient evidence for the full in-scope period, and no unresolved mandatory or critical/high breach. Missing material evidence means NOT DEMONSTRATED, not compliant.
Non-Compliance Triggers: Failure includes omitted material topic, unsupported target/claim, inconsistent boundary, unreliable data, ignored adverse impact, greenwashing, missing approval or unresolved assurance finding.
Typical Applicability / SBU: Group and entities with stakeholder or regulatory reporting
